**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health.**  
I’m here to support you as you navigate the many emotions that come with caring for a new baby.  

Today we’ll be using the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)** – a short, validated questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week. It’s not a diagnosis; it simply gives us a clearer picture of your mood, anxiety, and any thoughts you might be experiencing, so we can tailor support to what you need right now.  

Everything you share is completely confidential, and this is a safe, non‑judgmental space. My goal is to listen, validate, and work with you to ensure you feel supported.  

The EPDS consists of **10 brief questions**. I’ll ask each one in turn, and you can answer as honestly as you feel comfortable. If any question feels difficult, just let me know – we can pause or talk about it further.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

**First question:**  
*In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?*

I’ve found it hard to laugh or see the funny side of things lately. It’s only on the rare occasions—maybe once or twice in the whole week—that something actually makes me smile. Most of the time I just feel flat and don’t notice the humor around me.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Honestly, I haven’t really been able to laugh much lately. Most days I feel pretty flat, and it’s hard for me to see the funny side of things. It’s only on very rare moments—maybe once or twice in the whole week—that something actually makes me smile.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I haven’t really felt that excitement or enjoyment looking forward to things. Most of the time I just go through the motions, and only on a few rare occasions does something feel a bit enjoyable. It’s been mostly flat for me this past week.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I do find myself blaming myself a lot when something doesn’t go as planned. I keep thinking I’m not doing enough or that I’m a bad mother, even when the situation is out of my control. It happens fairly often—more than just an occasional thought, but not every single time. It leaves me feeling guilty and inadequate.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, I’ve been feeling anxious and worried a lot, even when there isn’t a clear reason. I keep thinking something might go wrong with the baby or that I’m not doing enough, and those worries hang around even though I try to calm myself down later. It’s been happening quite often this past week.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I’ve definitely had moments where I felt scared or even a bit panicky for no clear reason. It’s not every day, but it happens several times a week—especially when I’m alone with the baby and my mind starts racing about what could go wrong. I can usually calm myself down after a little while, but those sudden spikes of fear are pretty unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, I’ve been feeling like things are getting on top of me quite a bit. Between caring for the baby, trying to keep the house in order, and all the worries that keep popping up, I often feel overwhelmed. It’s not every single moment, but most days I’m struggling to keep everything from piling up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve been feeling really unhappy lately, and it’s been hard to get any decent sleep. Some nights I can’t fall asleep at all, and on other nights I wake up several times and can’t get back to sleep. It feels like my mind is racing with worries and sadness, so even when I’m exhausted, I just end up lying awake for hours. This has happened on several nights this past week.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yes, I’ve been feeling sad and miserable most days this past week. It’s hard to shake the heaviness, and even when I try to do something that used to make me happy, the sadness just stays with me.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve found myself crying several times this week—usually when the worries feel overwhelming or when I’m just exhausted. It’s not constant, but those moments come up a few times, and I can’t seem to stop the tears once they start.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts of harming myself.

I hear how overwhelming the past week has felt for you-struggling to find joy, feeling constant worry, guilt about motherhood, sadness, crying, and sleepless nights. It's understandable that caring for a newborn while coping with these emotions can feel exhausting and isolating.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no laughter, only rare moments, matching 'Not at all' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports little to no enjoyment or excitement looking forward to things, matching 'Hardly at all'.</sym>, <sym>The mother reports blaming herself fairly often—more than occasional but not all the time—matching 'Yes, some of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling anxious and worried a lot, frequently over the past week, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling scared/panicky several times a week, indicating occasional but not constant episodes, which aligns with 'Yes, sometimes'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent feeling of being overwhelmed, indicating 'Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>The mother reports frequent unhappiness and persistent sleep problems almost every night, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad and miserable most days, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>The patient describes crying several times this week, not constantly, which aligns with 'Only occasionally'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your responses indicate high scores on items reflecting <sym>anhedonia</sym> (Q1=3), loss of anticipatory pleasure (Q2=3), frequent self‑blame (Q3=2), pervasive worry (Q4=3), panic‑like fear (Q5=2), feeling overwhelmed (Q6=2), severe insomnia (Q7=3), persistent sadness (Q8=3), and crying episodes (Q9=2). The total EPDS score of 23 exceeds the ≥14 threshold that signals probable postpartum depression and warrants urgent referral. According to <med>DSM‑5</med> criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, you meet several core symptoms (depressed mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, guilt, diminished concentration) lasting more than two weeks and causing functional impairment. The absence of self‑harm thoughts (Q10=0) is reassuring but ongoing monitoring is needed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with your primary care provider to discuss these findings
2. Request a referral to a perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive assessment and possible therapy
3. Consider evidence‑based psychotherapy such as cognitive‑behavioral therapy or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression
4. Implement sleep hygiene strategies: limit caffeine, create a calming bedtime routine, and seek support for nighttime caregiving
5. Develop a safety plan and identify supportive contacts; if thoughts of self‑harm emerge, call emergency services or a crisis line immediately
6. Connect with community resources such as postpartum support groups or parenting classes for additional social support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: **Postpartum Mood & Anxiety Screening – Summary**

**Client Identifier:** [Redacted]  
**Date of Screening:** [Insert Date]  
**Clinician:** [Licensed Mental Health Professional]

---

### 1. Reported Symptoms & Emotional/Behavioral Concerns
| Item | Client Report | Symptom Category |
|------|----------------|------------------|
| **Anhedonia / Low Mood** | Rare ability to laugh; flat affect most days; difficulty seeing humor. | Diminished pleasure, low affect |
| **Loss of Anticipatory Enjoyment** | Little excitement or enjoyment looking forward to activities; “going through the motions.” | Anhedonia, reduced motivation |
| **Self‑Blame / Guilt** | Frequent self‑critical thoughts, feeling “bad mother,” guilt despite circumstances. | Excessive guilt, low self‑worth |
| **Generalized Anxiety** | Persistent worry about baby’s safety and adequacy; worries “hang around.” | Anxiety, rumination |
| **Panic / Fear Spikes** | Several episodes per week of sudden fear or panic, especially when alone with baby. | Panic‑like symptoms |
| **Feeling Overwhelmed** | Overwhelmed by caregiving, household tasks, and intrusive worries; most days. | Stress, perceived inability to cope |
| **Sleep Disturbance** | Difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep; racing thoughts; multiple awakenings; several nights per week. | Insomnia linked to mood/anxiety |
| **Sadness / Dysphoria** | Sad, miserable most days; heaviness persists despite attempts at pleasant activities. | Persistent low mood |
| **Crying Episodes** | Crying several times during the week, often triggered by overwhelming worries or exhaustion. | Emotional dysregulation |
| **Suicidal Ideation** | Denies any thoughts of self‑harm. | No current SI |

---

### 2. Consistent Patterns Across Responses
- **Persistent low mood** with limited positive affect (laughing, enjoyment).  
- **Elevated guilt/self‑criticism** concerning maternal role.  
- **Frequent anxiety** (worry, panic‑type fear) that is not clearly situational.  
- **Feelings of being overwhelmed** and difficulty managing daily demands.  
- **Sleep disruption** that appears secondary to rumination and anxiety.  
- **Crying and sadness** occurring multiple times per week.  

These patterns collectively suggest significant depressive‑type symptoms co‑occurring with anxiety‑type symptoms.

---

### 3. Screening Significance (Postpartum Depression / Anxiety)
- **Core depressive indicators:** Anhedonia, pervasive sadness, crying spells, insomnia.  
- **Core anxiety indicators:** Excessive worry, panic‑like episodes, feeling on edge, heightened physiological arousal.  
- **Maternal self‑efficacy concerns:** Persistent self‑blame and guilt are common contributors to postpartum mood disturbance.  
- **Functional impact:** Overwhelm and sleep loss may impair caregiving capacity and daily functioning.  

---

### 4. Highlighted Risk Factors
- **Persistent sadness & loss of pleasure** – present daily.  
- **Crying spells** – several times per week.  
- **Sleep difficulties** – insomnia with racing thoughts, multiple nights per week.  
- **Feelings of worthlessness/guilt** – frequent self‑critical thoughts about parenting.  
- **Anxiety & panic symptoms** – frequent worry and occasional panic‑like fear episodes.  
- **Overwhelm/Stress** – reported most days.  
- **Suicidal ideation:** **Absent** (no self‑harm thoughts reported).  

*Safety Note:* No current suicidal ideation; continue routine safety monitoring.

---

### 5. Screening Observation Summary
The client reports a constellation of depressive symptoms (marked anhedonia, pervasive sadness, frequent crying, insomnia) together with significant anxiety manifestations (excessive worry, intermittent panic‑type fear, feeling overwhelmed). Self‑blame and guilt regarding maternal competence are prominent. No suicidal thoughts are present at this time. The symptom profile aligns with clinically significant postpartum mood and anxiety concerns warranting further assessment and appropriate follow‑up.
